title.en: Drawing with a ruler and compass

text.en: Can you draw a smiling face, a wavy line, or a house with a ruler and compass instead of guessing by eye? In this chapter we learn what a compass can do, why a circle is a set of points at the same distance from a centre, and how that single idea helps us construct exact squares, rectangles and other figures without trial and error.

A compass has a fixed point that stays on the paper and a pencil end that moves. We open it against a ruler to set the distance between the two tips, and then turn it to draw a curve. If we mark every point that is 4 cm from a point P, they form a circle. P is called the centre and the distance from P to any point on the circle is the radius. Curves are shapes drawn without lifting the pencil. They include straight lines, circles and wavy shapes. Because the fixed tip does not move, every point drawn by the pencil is at the same distance, the radius, from the centre. That is why the compass draws a perfect circle.
Many pictures are built from circles and parts of circles, called arcs. A wavy line along a central line AB of 8 cm can be drawn as half circles. Each half circle has a diameter on AB, so the radius is half of that part. The challenge in a drawing like A Person is deciding where to put the compass tip and what radius to use. You can fix the radius and try different positions of the tip, or estimate from the picture. Ruler and compass together make artwork neater than freehand, and you can design your own patterns by changing the centre and the radius.
In a rectangle ABCD, A, B, C and D are the corners, AB, BC, CD and DA are the sides, and the angles are angle A, B, C and D. AB and CD are a pair of opposite sides. A rectangle has two properties: R1, opposite sides are equal in length, and R2, all angles are 90 degrees. A square has S1, all sides equal, and S2, all angles 90 degrees. A rectangle can be named by going around its corners in order from any corner, so ABCD, BCDA and DCBA are valid names, but ABDC is not because it jumps across the figure. A square or rectangle tilted on the page is still a square or rectangle; rotating does not change its sides or angles.
To construct a rectangle with sides of 5 cm and 3 cm, draw the side DC of 5 cm. At D and C construct lines perpendicular to DC, making 90 degree angles. On each perpendicular mark a point 3 cm from D and C. Rather than moving a ruler by trial, draw an arc of radius 3 cm from D and note where it cuts the perpendicular. Join the two new points and check R1 and R2: opposite sides should be equal and all angles 90 degrees. If a diagonal and a side are given, we use a circle. Draw DC, then a perpendicular at C. The point B on that line is at the diagonal length from D, so draw a circle or arc with centre D and radius equal to the diagonal; it cuts the line at B. Only the arc near the line is needed, not the whole circle. Finally construct perpendiculars at D and B; where they meet is the fourth corner A.
In the house figure, every border line is 5 cm, so the point A must be 5 cm from both B and C. Finding it with a ruler needs trial and error. With a compass, draw an arc of radius 5 cm with centre B and another arc of 5 cm with centre C. The point where the arcs meet is exactly 5 cm from both, so it is A. We only need small arcs near the meeting point, not full circles. Then join A to B and A to C. This idea of using circles to find a point at a given distance from one or two points is the key trick of all constructions in this chapter.
After constructing, check by measuring. In a rectangle the opposite sides should match and every angle should read 90 degrees on the protractor. A rectangle whose diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45 and 45 degrees has equal sides, so it is a square. If a construction is not accurate, the usual cause is that the compass radius slipped, so keep the compass tight and re-check the radius against the ruler.

problem.en: Construct a rectangle ABCD with DC = 5 cm and BC = 3 cm.

text.en: Draw DC = 5 cm with the ruler.
At D and C construct perpendiculars to DC.
With radius 3 cm, draw an arc from D and from C to cut the perpendiculars at A and B.

why.en: The compass gives equal lengths without trial and error.

text.en: Join A and B and check.

why.en: Opposite sides are equal and all angles 90 degrees.

problem.en: How do we find a point A that is 5 cm from both B and C?

text.en: Open the compass to 5 cm.

why.en: The radius is the required distance.

text.en: Draw an arc with centre B and another with centre C.

why.en: Each arc is all points 5 cm from its centre.

text.en: Mark the point where the arcs cross as A.

why.en: It lies on both arcs, so it is 5 cm from both.

problem.en: Construct a rectangle with a side of 4 cm and a diagonal of 8 cm.

text.en: Draw side DC = 4 cm and a perpendicular at C.
With centre D and radius 8 cm draw an arc to cut the perpendicular at B.
Draw perpendiculars at D and B; their meeting point is A.

problem.en: What radius gives a half circle on AB = 8 cm if the wave is one half circle across the whole line?

text.en: The half circle runs from A to B, so its diameter is 8 cm.

why.en: Diameter is the width of the circle.

text.en: Radius = 8 / 2 = 4 cm.
The centre X is the middle of AB, so AX = 4 cm.

why.en: The centre lies halfway along the line.

prompt.en: Explain how a compass draws a circle and how it helps find a point at a given distance.

requiredIdeas.en: The fixed tip is the centre and the pencil end is at a fixed distance, the radius.
All points on the circle are the same distance from the centre.
To find a point at a given distance from one or two points, draw circles or arcs of that radius and look where they meet.
This avoids trial and error with a ruler.

commonMisconceptions.en: Letting the compass radius change while drawing.
Drawing a full circle when only a small arc is needed.
Naming a rectangle with corners out of order.
Forgetting to check the 90 degree angles after drawing.

points.en: A compass draws a circle: the fixed tip is the centre and the distance to the pencil is the radius.
All points on a circle are the same distance from its centre.
A rectangle has equal opposite sides and four 90 degree angles; a square has all sides equal and four 90 degree angles.
Corners of a figure are named in order around it, so ABCD is valid but ABDC is not.
To find a point at a given distance from a point, draw an arc of that radius.
The point where two arcs meet is the same distance from both centres, and this builds rectangles and other figures exactly.
